meta.context: Parent raising kids who are learning English and wants them to sound more native. No linguistics background assumed.
meta.original_question: how to teach my kids to speak English more natively?
meta.working_question: What kind of English exposure actually changes how my kids speak — and which parts of "sounding native" are still movable at their age?
meta.triage_summary: The original invited tips any parenting blog could supply, left "more natively" ambiguous across four different targets (accent, grammar, vocabulary, idiom) that move on different timetables, and assumed the goal — whether native-likeness is even the right target is itself a live dispute. Revised to split the movable from the less-movable and to force choosing between rival accounts: more input, richer input, earlier input, or a different target altogether.
meta.staleness_note: The underlying studies are stable classics (1999–2018); staleness risk is low. Re-check only if a major new critical-period study lands.

root.label: What moves the needle?
root.note: Sharpened from "how to teach my kids to speak English more natively?" — split into which parts of sounding native are still movable, and what kind of exposure moves them.

questions.label: Native — meaning what?
questions.question: "More natively" — do you mean accent, grammar, vocabulary, or idiom? Pick the one that bothers you when you hear it. Would your kids agree it's a problem — and native like WHOM, exactly?
questions.single_reading_reason: One reading suffices — the card's work is a decision you make, and the reading exists to clear myths out of the way of it, not to add a second account.
questions.check_first: Search "François Grosjean" alone. What did he do before writing blogs, and does a blog by a career researcher carry different weight than a blog by a parenting site?
questions.read_for: Which of the listed myths you currently believe. Note the claim that most of the world's bilinguals are dominant in one language — and ask what that does to "native in both" as a target.
questions.level: Easy — a short readable blog post. The work is the decision it forces, not the reading. ~15 min.

questions.label: How open is the window?
questions.question: The largest study ever run on this — two-thirds of a million English speakers — found grammar-learning ability stays high until around 17. If the window is that open, why do kids who start at 5 still end up sounding different from kids who start at 15?
questions.check_first: This study collected its data through a viral internet grammar quiz. Search "Hartshorne critical period quiz methodology criticism" — find one objection to learning from a viral quiz before you lean on the result.
questions.read_for: What was measured: GRAMMAR judgments, not accent, not vocabulary. Note the age the learning-rate cliff actually sits at, and how long they estimate reaching the ceiling takes. Both numbers should surprise you.
questions.level: Middle. The paper's middle is computational modelling — skip it. Abstract, figures, and discussion carry what you need. ~35 min.

questions.label: Why did video deliver zero?
questions.question: Nine-month-old babies learned Mandarin sounds from a live person in twelve short sessions. Babies shown the SAME person saying the SAME things on video learned nothing at all. Why would a screen — identical input — deliver zero?
questions.single_reading_reason: One reading because the finding IS one experiment, and its force comes from the clean live-vs-video contrast. A second account would blur exactly the edge that makes it useful.
questions.check_first: Search "Patricia Kuhl TED talk" — she has explained this study to lay audiences herself. Watching it first is legitimate scaffolding; then read the paper to see what the talk smoothed over.
questions.read_for: The live-vs-recorded contrast and the authors' own explanation of WHY. Then note the participants' age, and write down — before anyone tells you — your best argument for and against this applying to a school-age child.
questions.level: Technical — a real PNAS paper with methods and statistics. The figures plus the discussion section carry it. ~40 min.

questions.label: Same years, different results
questions.question: Two kids, same school, same number of years in English. One sounds nearly native, one doesn't. The research measured what differs between such kids — how much of it turns out to be things a parent controls, and how much is the kid?
questions.check_first: Search "Johanne Paradis child English second language" — what population does she mostly study, and how similar is it to your household's situation?
questions.read_for: The list of what "richness of the English environment" actually consisted of — it is concrete and shorter than you'd guess — and the honest headline that child-internal factors explained more of the variance. Hold both.
questions.level: Middle — an academic paper, but the factor tables are readable and carry the payload. ~35 min.

questions.label: Clock, exposure, or wrong target?
questions.question: Three serious positions, all evidence-backed: (a) there's a sharp age cliff, so timing is everything; (b) the age effect on grammar largely dissolves once you control for education and use — so it's exposure, not a clock; (c) chasing native-likeness at all is the wrong goal, because a bilingual is not two monolinguals in one. They can't all govern your house. State the one you end up rejecting, fairly enough that its holder would sign it.
questions.check_first: Search "native speakerism criticism" and, separately, "critical period hypothesis defense". Both camps have serious people. Find one name on each side who is not in your source list.
questions.read_for: Cook: the argument that L2 users are speakers in their own right, not failed natives — and what he says classrooms should do differently. Then re-read Flege's abstract asking one question: what happened to the grammar-age effect when confounds were controlled?
questions.level: Technical in the values-wearing-empirical-clothes way. Sort each claim into "testable" or "a choice about goals" before picking a side. ~50 min including re-reading.

questions.label: How is "native" measured?
questions.question: "Sounds native" feels obvious to your ear — but how do researchers actually measure it? In the classic study, 240 speakers were rated by listeners for accent. What would your kids' recordings score, and what would count as "made it"?
questions.check_first: The reachable copy is hosted on a university course page, not the journal. Search the paper's title plus "Journal of Memory and Language" to confirm the course copy matches a real published article before citing it.
questions.read_for: How the accent ratings were collected and what the accent-vs-age curve looks like. Then the abstract's second finding: what happened to the GRAMMAR effect under controls — and why that split matters more than either result alone.
questions.level: Middle — long paper, but abstract, method sketch, and two figures carry it. ~35 min.

questions.label: Does immersion research transfer?
questions.question: Nearly every study here follows immigrants immersed in an English-speaking country. If English isn't the language of your street and playground, which findings still transfer to your house — and which quietly assumed twelve hours a day of free immersion?
questions.single_reading_reason: Thinking-only card: the work is auditing the earlier studies' settings against your own, and a new reading would just add another setting to audit.
questions.read_for: N/A — for each of Q2–Q4, write one line: where were these kids living, and how many waking hours of English did the setting hand them for free?
questions.level: No reading — ~20 min of thinking with the earlier cards open.

questions.label: What changes next week?
questions.question: Suppose the honest summary is: grammar and vocabulary stay open for years, accent mostly set earlier, live interaction beats screens, and "native" may be the wrong finish line. What actually changes in your house next week — and what were you about to spend effort on that this answer says to drop?
questions.single_reading_reason: Thinking-only card by design; attaching a reading would hand over the judgment it exists to provoke.
questions.read_for: N/A — name one thing you'll start, one you'll stop, and one worry you're allowed to put down. Say them out loud to someone.
questions.level: No reading — ~20 min, best done out loud.

S1.citation: A Critical Period for Second Language Acquisition: Evidence from 2/3 Million English Speakers · Hartshorne, Tenenbaum & Pinker · 2018 · Cognition · peer-reviewed article
S1.verified_how: Search confirmed title, authors, year, venue, N (669,498), and core claim (grammar-learning ability preserved to ~17.4, then declines; measured by grammaticality quiz). Link is the author page with open PDF; journal copy is paywalled.
S1.complexity: Quantitative — computational modelling middle; abstract, figures and discussion carry it

S2.citation: Foreign-Language Experience in Infancy: Effects of Short-Term Exposure and Social Interaction on Phonetic Learning · Kuhl, Tsao & Liu · 2003 · PNAS 100, 9096–9101 · peer-reviewed article
S2.verified_how: Search confirmed title, authors, year, venue, pages, and core claim (9-month-olds learned Mandarin phonetics from live tutors but not from audio/video of the same material).
S2.complexity: Structure — real methods and stats; figures plus discussion carry it

S3.citation: Age Constraints on Second-Language Acquisition · Flege, Yeni-Komshian & Liu · 1999 · Journal of Memory and Language 41, 78–104 · peer-reviewed article
S3.verified_how: Search confirmed title, authors, year, venue, pages, design (240 Korean speakers, accent ratings + grammaticality test), and core claims (accent worsens steadily with age of arrival; the grammar-age effect became nonsignificant once confounded variables were controlled). Link is a university course copy; the journal copy is paywalled — Q6's check_first tells the reader to confirm the copy matches.
S3.complexity: Quantitative — long; abstract, method sketch and two figures suffice

S4.citation: Going Beyond the Native Speaker in Language Teaching · Cook · 1999 · TESOL Quarterly 33(2), 185–209 · peer-reviewed article
S4.verified_how: Search confirmed title, author, year, venue, volume and pages, and core argument (L2 users are speakers in their own right, not approximations to monolingual natives; teaching should target the successful L2 user).
S4.paired_with: The ERIC record (eric.ed.gov, EJ587954) summarises it, and full-text copies circulate on academia.edu under the exact title — search the title verbatim
S4.complexity: Levels of meaning — an argument essay, not a study; extract the claims and their warrant

S5.citation: Individual Differences in Child English Second Language Acquisition: Comparing Child-Internal and Child-External Factors · Paradis · 2011 · Linguistic Approaches to Bilingualism 1, 213–237 · peer-reviewed article
S5.verified_how: Search confirmed title, author, year, venue, pages, and core claims (aptitude, age, L1 typology, length of exposure and environment richness all predicted outcomes; child-internal factors explained more variance than external ones).
S5.complexity: Structure — factor tables carry the payload

S6.citation: Myths About Bilingualism · Grosjean · 2010, maintained · Psychology Today "Life as a Bilingual" blog · named-researcher explainer
S6.verified_how: Search confirmed author, venue, series, and content (myth list including no-delay finding, code-switching as adaptation, most bilinguals dominant in one language).
S6.complexity: Deliberately easy; the work is the decision it forces

teach_back.question: You keep saying you want the kids to sound more native — native like who? And how would you know when they'd made it?
If you could only pick one: an hour of English cartoons a day, or ten minutes of real back-and-forth conversation — which, and why?
Straight answer: is it too late for them? What's still open at their age and what's mostly closed?
